name: Reddish Brick
lede: Reddish Brick is ColorHub's English name for Benikaba, a dark red-orange that Japanese tradition names for the bark of the red birch, close enough to this hue's nearest library neighbor that the two are easy to mistake.

sections.title: Red birch, not brick
sections.body:
Wikipedia's list of traditional Japanese colors gives this swatch as Benikaba (紅樺), combining beni, "crimson," with kaba, "birch," naming the reddish bark of the red birch tree [1]. ColorHub's English rendering, Reddish Brick, reaches for a building material rather than the birch bark the Japanese name describes [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 places the swatch in block 38, "dark reddish orange," about 5.5 units from that block's centre [2]. The library's nearest other named color is literally [[brick]] itself, just 3.0 units away, which makes the English rendering an understandable, if inexact, choice [2].

Measured in LCH it reads lightness 36, chroma 57, hue 36 degrees, a dark, strongly saturated red-orange [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match in 414 of 23,781 paintings, under 2 percent, as photographed [3]. It plays a mid-tone role in 79 percent of its occurrences, rarely a shadow or highlight [3]. Juan Correa de Vivar and Albrecht Dürer each carry it at about six times the archive's overall rate [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the color word Carmine, at over 30 times the ordinary rate, and its presence peaks in the 1480s, in 17 of 141 paintings [3].
